text: Lesson 29 proved Tier 1's failover plan works for a clean database and routing failure. That doesn't prove checkout survives a slow dependency while it's still running, or that the team itself knows what to do during a real outage rather than just owning a script. This lab runs both tests: a real chaos experiment, and a structured game day.

The experiment starts with a hypothesis, stated before anything runs: if payment-integration's gateway calls exceed two seconds, checkout-api's circuit breaker should open within ten seconds and fall back to pay on delivery instead of hanging. A steady state is confirmed first -- checkout success at or above 99.5 percent -- because without that baseline there's no way to say afterward whether the experiment actually proved anything.

Abort criteria are written down and agreed on before injection starts, not decided in the moment things start hurting: checkout success dropping below 98 percent, any order charged twice, or simply any engineer calling it off in the chaos room. The blast radius is capped at five percent of production traffic. Deciding this in advance means nobody has to argue mid-experiment about whether to stop.

Injecting 2.5 seconds of latency on a 5 percent canary slice, the circuit breaker opened at eight seconds -- inside the ten-second hypothesis -- and checkout fell back to pay on delivery cleanly. Checkout success held at 99.6 percent throughout. The hypothesis was confirmed by a measurement, not assumed because the architecture diagram said it should work.

The game day tests the people, not the code. The team is briefed that East US 2 has gone fully unreachable, roles are assigned -- incident commander, scribe, comms lead, ops -- and the scribe's real timestamped log shows the incident commander calling for failover at 10:03 and Lesson 29's script restoring health by 10:09. Chapter 7's blameless debrief follows immediately, reviewing what the plan missed, not who executed it.

The moment that matters most isn't the failover completing on time -- it's the incident commander asking, at 10:11, whether anything else was silently depending on East US 2, and nobody on the call being able to answer for certain. That open question is exactly where Lesson 31's case study picks up.
